description: HTML document structure and semantic elements

screens.body:
HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language, but forget the fancy name. 'Markup' just means you mark up plain text with tags so the browser knows what each part is. A tag like

says 'this is a paragraph.' Most tags come in pairs: an opening tag and a closing tag with a slash.

options: Mark up text so the browser knows what each part is
check.question: HTML tags…

screens.heading: HTML is markup, not magic
screens.keyPoint: Tags label your content so the browser understands it.

screens.body: Every HTML page has the same skeleton. It starts with <!DOCTYPE html>, then an <html> tag wrapping everything. Inside, the <head> holds behind-the-scenes info like the page title. The <body> holds everything you actually see — text, images, buttons. If it's visible, it lives in the body.
screens.heading: The skeleton of every page
screens.keyPoint: Head is behind the scenes; body is what you see.

screens.body:

screens.keyPoint: h1 for the main heading, p for text, a with href for links.

screens.body: Attributes live inside the opening tag and add details. An image tag needs src (where the picture is) and alt (a text description). Alt text matters: screen readers read it aloud for people who can't see the image, and it shows if the picture fails to load. Always write meaningful alt text.

options: It describes the image for screen readers
It must always be left empty
check.question: The alt attribute on an image…

screens.heading: Attributes add details
screens.keyPoint: Attributes add info; alt text describes images for everyone.

screens.body: Semantic elements say what a section IS, not just how it looks. <header> is the top of the page, <nav> holds navigation links, <main> holds the main content, <footer> is the bottom. Using them instead of plain <div> boxes helps screen readers and search engines understand your page.

options: It says 'this is navigation' to browsers and screen readers
check.question: Why use <nav> instead of <div>?

screens.heading: Semantic elements say what things ARE
screens.keyPoint: Semantic tags describe meaning, not just appearance.

screens.body: When the browser reads your HTML, it builds a tree of objects called the DOM — the Document Object Model. Each element becomes a node with parents, children, and siblings. This tree is what JavaScript will grab onto later to change the page. Think of it as the family tree of your page.

options: The browser's tree of your page's elements
check.question: The DOM is…

screens.heading: The DOM: your page as a tree
screens.keyPoint: The DOM is the browser's tree version of your HTML.

screens.body:
HTML has rules, and the W3C validator checks your page against them for free. The most common mistakes: forgetting a closing tag, and closing tags in the wrong order — like

Hi there

. Tags must close in reverse order, like stacking bowls. Valid HTML behaves predictably everywhere.

screens.heading: Valid HTML passes the test
screens.keyPoint: Close tags in reverse order; validate with the W3C checker.
